title: Are Free Nights Electricity Plans Worth It? (2026)
h1: Are free nights electricity plans worth it?
desc: Free nights electricity plans can backfire if you use power mostly by day. See the break-even math and find out who actually saves.
lede: Free nights electricity plans are worth it mainly if you can shift roughly half or more of your monthly usage into the free window, such as charging an EV or running appliances overnight. For typical daytime-heavy households, the higher daytime rate that funds the free hours often makes these plans cost more, not less, than a flat-rate plan.
body:
How free nights and weekends plans actually price your electricity

Free nights plans don't give away electricity. They shift the cost. The retail provider sets a higher energy charge for daytime hours, then waives the energy charge during a set overnight window, often something like 9 p.m. to 6 a.m. Weekend versions add Saturday and Sunday to that free window.

Two details trip people up every time. First, the free period usually doesn't cover the early evening, which is when most households use the most electricity: cooking, laundry, lights, and air conditioning or heating recovering from the day. Second, delivery charges from your local utility (the TDU in Texas) apply to every kilowatt-hour you use, day or night. Only the energy charge is waived, not the full bill.

That means the real question isn't whether the plan sounds generous. It's whether enough of your actual usage lands inside the free window to offset the higher rate you pay the rest of the time. Before comparing any plan, it helps to know what a normal household even uses in a month; see how many kWh a house uses per month for typical ranges.

The break-even math: when a free nights plan actually pays off

Here's a worked example using realistic Texas delivery charges so you can see exactly where the savings come from, and where they disappear.

Assumptions for this example (illustrative numbers, not a specific offer):

  • Household uses 1,000 kWh in the month
  • Plan A (free nights): 21.0 cents/kWh energy charge during the day, $0 energy charge at night, $9.95 monthly base charge
  • Plan B (flat rate): 11.0 cents/kWh energy charge all day, $9.95 monthly base charge
  • Both plans are delivered by CenterPoint Energy, which charges 4.972 cents/kWh plus a $4.99 fixed delivery fee on every kWh, regardless of time of use

Plan B: flat rate, 1,000 kWh

Energy: 1,000 kWh × $0.11 = $110.00
Delivery: 1,000 kWh × $0.04972 = $49.72
Fixed charges: $9.95 + $4.99 = $14.94
Total: $174.66 (an all-in average of 17.47 cents/kWh)

Plan A: free nights, 35% of usage overnight (350 kWh free, 650 kWh billed)

Energy: 650 kWh × $0.21 = $136.50
Delivery: 1,000 kWh × $0.04972 = $49.72 (applies to all usage, including the free hours)
Fixed charges: $14.94
Total: $201.16 (26.50 cents/kWh effective daytime rate drags the average up)

At a 35% overnight usage split, the free nights plan costs about $26 more than the flat-rate plan. The free hours didn't cover enough of the bill to beat the higher daytime rate.

Finding the break-even point

Using the same assumptions, the free nights plan only matches the flat-rate plan's $174.66 total once about 48% of the household's monthly usage happens inside the free window. Below that share, the flat rate wins. Above it, free nights wins, and the savings grow fast as more usage shifts overnight.

Share of usage at night (free)Free nights plan totalFlat rate plan totalCheaper option
20%$232.66$174.66Flat rate
35%$201.16$174.66Flat rate
48%$173.86$174.66About even
60%$148.66$174.66Free nights
80%$106.66$174.66Free nights

The lesson: free nights plans reward households that genuinely move a majority of their usage into the overnight hours. They punish households whose usage is spread evenly across the day, because the daytime rate you pay the rest of the time is set high enough to fund the free hours.

Who actually benefits from free nights plans

A handful of usage patterns can realistically clear that 45-50% overnight threshold:

  • EV owners who charge at home overnight. A single overnight charging session can easily add 20 to 40+ kWh, which can dominate a household's total monthly usage and push a big share of it into the free window. See how much it costs to charge an EV at home to estimate your own charging load.
  • Households that run pool pumps, water heaters, or laundry on delayed timers overnight. These are large, schedulable loads that don't need to run during the day.
  • Genuine night owls and some night-shift households who are awake, cooking, running electronics, and heating or cooling the home during the free hours rather than during the day.
  • Homes with smart thermostats that pre-cool or pre-heat overnight to reduce daytime HVAC runtime, shifting part of that load into the free window.

Who should probably skip them

If your household looks like a typical 9-to-5 family, free nights plans usually cost more. Daytime-heavy usage includes:

  • Work-from-home households running computers, lighting, and HVAC all day
  • Families with daytime air conditioning or heating needs while someone is home
  • Homes where most cooking, laundry, and appliance use happens in the evening before the free window starts

In these cases, a straightforward flat-rate plan, or a time-of-use plan with a smaller day/night spread, usually beats a free nights plan. For a broader look at how fixed and variable pricing structures compare, read fixed vs variable electricity rates in Texas.

How to check a specific free nights plan before you sign up

Don't rely on the marketing name. Every plan sold in a competitive market publishes an Electricity Facts Label (EFL), and in Texas it must show the average price per kWh at 500, 1,000, and 2,000 kWh of use. That average price already bakes in the higher daytime rate and the free hours together, so it's a faster gut check than doing the math yourself.

  1. Pull up the EFL and find the average price at the usage level closest to your own monthly kWh.
  2. Compare that average price to a flat-rate plan's average price at the same usage level.
  3. Check the exact free-hour window; some plans start free hours at 9 p.m., others at 10 p.m. or midnight, which matters if you go to bed early.
  4. Confirm whether delivery charges and the monthly base charge are counted in the free hours (they almost never are).

If you're not sure how to read these labels, walk through how to read an Electricity Facts Label (EFL) in Texas before comparing plans. It also helps to know what a reasonable price even looks like in your state; see what counts as a good price per kWh for context, and Texas TDU delivery charges for the fixed and per-kWh delivery fees that apply no matter which plan you pick.

What to do next

Add up roughly how much of your usage realistically happens overnight before you sign a free nights contract. If you charge an EV at home, run a pool pump on a timer, or are genuinely active at night, the math can work strongly in your favor. If your household is busiest during the day, run the same break-even comparison shown above using your own rate and usage, or compare current plans side by side for your area to see the all-in average price rather than the headline "free" offer.
faq: What hours count as free on a free nights electricity plan?

It varies by plan, but overnight windows commonly run from around 9 p.m. to 6 a.m., with some plans also including full weekend days. Always check the plan's Electricity Facts Label for the exact hours.
Do free nights plans really have zero delivery charges at night?
No. Delivery charges from your local utility apply to every kilowatt-hour you use at any time of day; only the energy charge from the retail provider is waived during free hours.
Are free nights plans a good fit for charging an EV at home?
Often yes, since a single overnight charge can account for a large share of your monthly usage, making it easier to clear the break-even point where free nights plans beat a flat rate.
How do I know if a free nights plan will actually save me money?

Compare the plan's average price per kWh at your typical monthly usage, listed on its Electricity Facts Label, against a flat-rate plan's average price at the same usage level, rather than trusting the word "free" alone.
